new_statements.quote: Nach betontem Vocal fällt auslautendes a oder o zuweilen ab, so: desê (dese[j]ar), plê (praia), santopê (centopêa), cjé (céo), sapé (chapéo), navi (navio) [...]. Meistens aber zieht in diesem Falle auslautendes a den Ton auf sich, so: boá (boa), camiá (*caminha, caminho), djá (dia), luá (rua), nuá (lua), quá (cousa). [p. 15] Sonst finde ich die letzte Silbe statt der vorletzten betont in Dessú (Deus), cumó, cablá (cabra), djividá, in den beiden letzten Fällen wohl aus Versehen. [p. 17] Das Santhomensische begünstigt die doppelte Wortgestalt ⏑́ – und – ⏑́, während das Angolensische der letzteren abgeneigt ist.
new_statements.translation: After a stressed vowel, final a or o sometimes drops, e.g. desê (desejar), plê (praia), santopê (centopeia), cjé (céu), sapé (chapéu), navi (navio) [...]. Mostly, however, in this case final a draws the stress onto itself, e.g. boá (boa), camiá (*caminha, caminho), djá (dia), luá (rua), nuá (lua), quá (cousa). [p. 15] Otherwise I find the last syllable stressed instead of the penultimate in Dessú (Deus), cumó, cablá (cabra), djividá, in the last two cases probably by mistake. [p. 17] Santomense favours the double word shape stressed-unstressed and unstressed-stressed, whereas the Angolan language is averse to the latter. (The two metrical symbols on p. 17 are printed as an accented breve followed by a dash and a dash followed by an accented breve.)

new_statements.relation_note: The catalog records Santome as a stress-vs-tone conflict (Ferraz 1979 stress language; Maurer 1995/2008 two-tone system, coded in APiCS 35-120). Schuchardt 1882 sits on the stress side: he marks word stress throughout, never mentions tone, and adds the earliest placement detail (both trochaic and iambic disyllables occur, with drift toward final stress). It does not resolve the conflict, and its evidence is second-hand (written texts from correspondents), so it refines rather than settles the record.
new_statements.rule_in_words: No rule is stated. Schuchardt marks stress word by word with an acute (inherited from the Portuguese etymon: sapé, navi, djelo, blato, mina, cloçon) and treats Santome as a stress language with no mention of tone. He says the language favours both disyllabic shapes, stressed-unstressed and unstressed-stressed, so no single position holds; the shifts he observes all go toward the final syllable (final -a attracts the stress in hiatus words: boá, djá, luá, nuá, quá; final instead of penultimate stress in Dessú, cumó). Placement is therefore lexically given (final or penult), not derivable from a phonological rule.
new_statements.exceptions: Final-syllable stress instead of the expected penult in Dessú (Deus), cumó, cablá (cabra), djividá, the last two 'probably by mistake' (p. 15); final -a attracting stress after loss of a consonant (boá, camiá, djá, luá, nuá, quá) versus final-vowel loss after a stressed vowel (desê, plê, sapé, navi) (p. 14); final-stressed trisyllabic nouns lose their first or second vowel (cloçon, djelo, póçon) while trisyllabic paroxytones lose the first (blato, mina) (p. 17). Caveat from p. 5: the texts and their accents came from correspondents' written material, which Schuchardt corrected 'only where I felt entirely sure'.
new_statements.identity_note: Schuchardt 1882 describes the creole of the island of São Tomé proper ('das Santhomensische', today Santome/Forro) from texts sent to him around 1882; he explicitly sets the Angolares apart (p. 4) and uses 'angolensisch' for Angolan (Kimbundu-shaped, from Cannecattim and Souza & Alves) material. His remarks that penultimate stress is regular and final stress rare in 'Angolensisch' (pp. 15, 18 fn. 1) concern that Angolan material, not Santome.

new_statements.quote: p. 531: "Primary stress usually fell on the penultimate syllable in nouns, but moved to the final syllable when that was heavy. Verbs were stressed on the final syllable." p. 540: "Primary stress fell on the penultimate syllable in nominal forms in which that syllable was light (e.g., *bla.su ‘arm’), but shifted to the last syllable when that was heavy (e.g., *bo.toN ‘button’). Verbs were always stressed on the final syllable (e.g., *be.be ‘to drink’). Therefore, a word’s morphological category must be considered during stress allocation." p. 541: "...as the ggpc was sensitive to syllabic weight for attributing stress, just as its daughter languages are. This topic, however, requires more attention in future investigations."

new_statements.relation_note: The catalog lists Santome with an empty rule and no existing statements. This article supplies a weight-sensitive, morphologically conditioned stress rule for the proto-language (penult default in nouns, final if heavy; verbs final) and states that the daughter languages, Santome included, are likewise weight-sensitive for stress; it does not give a dedicated synchronic stress rule for Santome, so it adds content compatible with (not contradicting) the empty catalog entry. The article's scope is GGPC plus all four daughters (Santome, Angolar, Lung'Ie, Fa d'Ambo).
new_statements.rule_in_words: The explicit rule is stated for the reconstructed Gulf of Guinea Proto-Creole (GGPC), not for modern Santome: in nouns primary stress is penultimate when the final syllable is light and final when the final syllable is heavy (coda N/S/liquid/glide); verbs (infinitives) are always final-stressed, so morphological category conditions stress. For the daughter languages (Santome, Angolar, Lung'Ie, Fa d'Ambo) the article only asserts in passing that they too are 'sensitive to syllabic weight for attributing stress' and flags the topic for future work (p. 541, again p. 553: 'the interaction of stress and syllable weight still requires further investigation'). Santome forms cited carry stress marks consistent with this: penult in disyllabic nouns/adjectives ([ˈklo.su] 'pit', [ˈpla.sɐ] 'square', [ˈplo.ko] 'pig', [ˈpɛ.tu] 'near', [ˈbɐ̃.kʊ] 'bench') and final in [bɐ̃ˈna] 'banana'.
new_statements.exceptions: Verbs always final-stressed (GGPC), attributed on p. 541 to the historically heavy (r-final) Portuguese infinitive syllable whose weight-assigned stress survived coda loss; Fa d'Ambo antepenultimate stress in [ˈfi.bi.li] < *fɛ.blɛ explained as stress assigned before copy-vowel anaptyxis (p. 540). Liquid loss/compensatory lengthening said to be independent of word stress in the daughter languages (p. 540, p. 551).
new_statements.identity_note: The article treats the reconstructed Gulf of Guinea Proto-Creole and its four daughters (Santome, Angolar, Lung'Ie, Fa d'Ambo) together; the explicit stress rule is for the proto-language (based on Bandeira 2017), with Santome data from fieldwork wordlists (523 Santome items). No Santome dialect is singled out.

readall_conflicts: The catalog's recorded conflict stands: Ferraz 1979 (and now, as the earliest witness, Schuchardt 1882) treat Santome as a stress language with lexically placed stress on the final or penultimate syllable, whereas Maurer 1995/2008 (followed by Hagemeijer's APiCS coding, 'Very certain') analyse it as a two-tone language. Schuchardt's accents come from correspondents' written texts, not from his own hearing, and he had no way to detect tone, so his testimony cannot weigh against Maurer's instrumental-era analysis; it only shows that the stress reading is the older one. Bandeira, Araujo & Finbow 2022 could not be opened (Brill bot wall on both attempts), so whatever it says about stress or vowel length in the daughter languages remains unread.

sources.note: A syllable-structure study of Santome by the author who argues (thesis 2000/2003: 87-88) that Ferraz failed to prove tonal opposition and that the system works with stress; likely states its prosodic assumptions (stress-marked transcriptions) in passing; tone content not seen.

tone.says: A syllable-structure study of Santome by the author who argues (thesis 2000/2003: 87-88) that Ferraz failed to prove tonal opposition and that the system works with stress; likely states its prosodic assumptions (stress-marked transcriptions) in passing; tone content not seen.
